body.heading: Small words, big help
paragraphs: Some verbs never work alone. They team up with an action word and help it do its job — a little like a friend who holds the ladder while you climb. These teammates are called helping verbs, and choosing the right one depends on who is doing the action.
Spark's rule is simple: he, she and it travel with is, does and has. I, you, we and they travel with am, are, do and have. Learn the teams once, and the right helper will start to feel automatic.

body.heading: The I, you, we and they team
paragraphs: I — am, do, have. I am ready. I do my chores. I have finished.
You — are, do, have. You are kind. You do great work. You have a turn next.
We — are, do, have. We are friends. We do it together. We have a plan.
They — are, do, have. They are coming. They do their best. They have two dogs.

body.heading: The he, she and it team
paragraphs: He — is, does, has. He is tall. He does his homework. He has a red bike.
She — is, does, has. She is reading. She does karate. She has a kind smile.
It — is, does, has. It is raining. It does look cloudy. It has four wheels.

body.heading: Words to know
paragraphs: Helping verb — a small verb that joins a main verb, like is in 'She is running'.
Main verb — the verb that carries the action, like running, reading or finished.
Subject — who or what the sentence is about: I, you, he, she, it, we or they.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Make up a silly sentence for each team: one with 'They have…' and one with 'It has…'. Which helper did you pick each time, and why?
2. Listen to people talking today. How many helping verbs can you catch in one conversation?

takeaway: He, she and it take is, does and has; I takes am, do and have; you, we and they take are, do and have.
